content: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is the most common rheumatic disease in children. Methotrexate, a drug with broad immunomodulatory properties, is the most frequently used disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) for this condition. This review is an update of a 2001 Cochrane review and contributes to a living guideline for managing JIA in children and adolescents. The objective of this review was to evaluate the benefits and harms of methotrexate in children and adolescents with JIA. The Australian JIA Living Guideline Working Group conducted a comprehensive search of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and trial registries, with the most recent search conducted on February 1, 2023. The inclusion criteria focused on RCTs comparing methotrexate with placebo, no treatment, or other DMARDs, with or without additional therapies, in individuals aged 18 years or younger with JIA. Standard Cochrane methods were used for data collection and analysis. The primary comparison was methotrexate versus placebo, and the outcomes assessed included treatment response, sustained clinically inactive disease, functional outcomes, pain, participant global assessment of well-being, serious adverse events, and withdrawals due to adverse events. The certainty of evidence for each outcome was evaluated using the GRADE approach. This update included three new trials, bringing the total to five RCTs with 575 participants. Three trials compared oral methotrexate with placebo, one compared methotrexate plus intra-articular glucocorticoid (IAGC) therapy with IAGC therapy alone, and one compared methotrexate with leflunomide. Methotrexate doses ranged from 5 mg/m²/week to 15 mg/m²/week in four trials, while one trial used a dose of 0.5 mg/kg/week. The trials included 31 to 226 participants, with an average age of 4 to 10 years. Most participants were female and had nonsystemic JIA. The trial involving methotrexate plus IAGC therapy focused on children with the oligoarticular subtype of JIA. Two placebo-controlled trials and the trial comparing methotrexate with leflunomide were adequately randomized and blinded, minimizing the risk of bias. However, one placebo-controlled trial lacked sufficient reporting of randomization methods, raising concerns about selection bias. The trial evaluating methotrexate plus IAGC therapy was susceptible to performance and detection biases. When comparing methotrexate with placebo, methotrexate may increase the number of children achieving a treatment response within six months (absolute difference of 163 more per 1000 people; risk ratio [RR] 1.67, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.21 to 2.31; low-certainty evidence). However, methotrexate may have little or no effect on pain (mean difference [MD] −1.10 points on a 0–100 scale, 95% CI −9.09 to 6.88), participant global assessment of well-being (absolute difference of 92 more per 1000 people; RR 1.23, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.72), serious adverse events (absolute difference of 5 fewer per 1000 people; RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.04 to 8.97), or withdrawals due to adverse events (RR 3.46, 95% CI 0.60 to 19.79). All outcomes were reported within six months of randomization. The certainty of evidence was downgraded to low due to indirectness (suboptimal methotrexate dosing and diverse outcome measures) and imprecision (small sample sizes and low event rates). No trials reported on functional outcomes or sustained clinically inactive disease. Serious adverse events included liver enzyme abnormalities, abdominal pain, and accidental overdose. When comparing methotrexate plus IAGC therapy with IAGC therapy alone, the combination may have little or no effect on the likelihood of sustained clinically inactive disease or the rate of withdrawals due to adverse events within 12 months in children with oligoarticular JIA (low-certainty evidence). No severe adverse events were reported, and the study did not assess treatment response, functional outcomes, pain, or participant global assessment of well-being. When comparing methotrexate with leflunomide, methotrexate may have little or no effect on treatment response, functional outcomes, participant global assessment of well-being, serious adverse events, or withdrawals due to adverse events within four months (low-certainty evidence). Pain and sustained clinically inactive disease were not reported in this study. In conclusion, oral methotrexate (5 mg/m²/week to 15 mg/m²/week) may increase the number of children achieving a treatment response compared with placebo but may have little or no effect on pain or participant global assessment of well-being. Methotrexate combined with IAGC injections may have little or no effect on the likelihood of sustained clinically inactive disease in children with oligoarticular JIA. Similarly, methotrexate may have little or no effect compared with leflunomide on treatment response, functional outcomes, or participant global assessment of well-being. Serious adverse events associated with methotrexate appear to be rare. This review will be updated as new evidence becomes available to inform the living guideline.
